title: Adiabatic realization of anomalous Floquet topological systems
authors: Luca Asteria, Marcel N. Kosch, Henrik P. Zahn, Jonathan Bracker, André Eckardt, Klaus Sengstock, Christof Weitenberg
abstract: Topology has emerged as a central concept for classifying phases of matter. The situation is especially rich in periodically driven systems, where anomalous Floquet topological phases break the usual bulk-boundary correspondence between Chern number and edges modes of two-dimensional systems. These phases were so far realized by periodic modulation of the tunneling elements at frequencies near-resonant with respect to the system's bandwidth, a regime where Floquet heating plays a significant role in interacting systems. Here we show that such anomalous Floquet topological phases can also be realized by means of an adiabatic protocol, where the system is always in the instantaneous ground state of the cyclic path in parameter space, like in a Thouless charge pump. We experimentally realize such a state using ultracold atoms in a hexagonal lattice where we adiabatically modulate the lattice geometry, including the sublattice offset. To infer the topology, we use the micromotion area in real-space, which was recently identified as a proxy for the winding number. This way of realizing anomalous phases avoids resonant Floquet heating and imperfect loading into the target state. We demonstrate the robustness of the adiabatic construction by observing the anomalous phase even in the presence of mean-field interactions of magnitude comparable to all other energy scales. These findings are promising for engineering novel topological states in a more robust way.
summary: The paper reports on the adiabatic realization of anomalous Floquet topological phases in ultracold atoms trapped in optical lattices. By slowly modulating the lattice geometry rather than driving near resonance, the researchers achieve robust control over these exotic quantum states. This method is significant because it offers a more stable and controllable pathway for engineering novel topological matter compared to existing techniques.
main_problem: The research aims to demonstrate an adiabatic method for realizing anomalous Floquet topological phases, circumventing the limitations of conventional near-resonant driving schemes.
main_result: Anomalous topological phases were successfully realized in ultracold atoms by adiabatically modulating the lattice geometry, showing robustness even in the presence of significant mean-field interactions.
method: The study combines theoretical analysis (using micromotion area as a winding number proxy) with experimental realization using ultracold atoms in optical lattices.
model_or_system: The system is modeled by atoms in a tunable honeycomb lattice, whose parameters ($J_i$, sublattice offset $\Delta$) are adiabatically modulated along a cyclic path in parameter space.
key_observables: Micromotion area (proxy for winding number), directed chiral edge transport, and relative sublattice population imbalance ($	ext{Na}-	ext{Nb}$).
important_parameters: Lattice geometry parameters ($J_1, J_2, J_3$, $\Delta$), driving frequency/period ($T_{	ext{drive}}$), and interaction strength ($U_H$).
main_assumptions: The adiabatic path keeps the system in the instantaneous ground state; measurements often involve approximations for detection efficiency or mean-field interactions.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the conceptual charge pump mechanism, experimental protocols involving lattice modulation steps, and measured trajectories/areas confirming the anomalous topological phase.
paper_structure: The paper progresses from establishing the theoretical link between Thouless pumping and anomalous Floquet topology to detailing the adiabatic protocol, measuring the topological invariant (micromotion area), and finally demonstrating robustness against interactions and disorder.
why_interesting: This work provides a highly controllable, experimentally viable platform for engineering exotic quantum phases of matter using ultracold atoms, moving beyond purely theoretical predictions in Floquet engineering.
